all.title: Interactive System Development Life Cycle Stages

concepts.name: extended reality
concepts.definition: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

defining_facts.text: Extended Reality (XR) is an umbrella term, not a specific technology, that covers all present or future immersive technologies, such as augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR).

The X in Extended Reality (XR) can be read as a variable, not only as part of 'extended', and its values such as A, V, and M denote augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR), and mixed reality (MR), while its many possible values form present or future immersive technologies.

Although adoption statistics can be misleading, earlier use forecasts discussed in the course indicate that extended reality, which covers augmented reality (AR) and virtual reality (VR), has commercial potential in video games (about 34% or more than one third of applications), healthcare, engineering, live events, video entertainment, real estate, retail, and military (about 4% of application areas, a figure that may change); because worldwide military budgets are huge, even 4% is a large monetary amount, so penetration in the commercial space can be expected both percentage-wise and value-wise.

concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: immersive experience
concepts.definition: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

defining_facts.text: An immersive experience is a perceived experience through sensory organs that appears real: when a person experiences an environment through sensory organs and fails to distinguish that environment from the person's real environment, perceiving it as the real environment, the technology producing that experience is an immersive technology.

concepts.name: field of view
concepts.definition: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.

defining_facts.text: Field of view (FOV) is a content-related factor in virtual reality (VR) that affects susceptibility to cybersickness (CS), and it is the extent to which the display in a VR headset captures the user's field of vision.
A larger field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) captures a larger field of vision and generally results in greater immersion.
Research has found that reducing the field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can be an effective way to alleviate symptoms of cybersickness (CS).

An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

Developer-side strategies for reducing cybersickness (CS) include field of view (FOV) adjustment, dynamic visual blur, rest frames, optical-flow manipulation, hardware-level alterations, and locomotion modifications.
Field of view (FOV) is the amount of virtual environment that is visible at any moment.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment can, ideally, mitigate the onset or severity of cybersickness (CS) because restricting the field of view reduces peripheral optical flow.
Field of view (FOV) adjustment has been found to be effective across genders without any negative impacts.

A drawback of field of view (FOV) adjustment is that it can reduce presence or sense of presence and impair performance in visual tasks because it restricts certain visual content, potentially degrading user experience.
A symmetric mask is a classical field of view (FOV) adjustment technique that occludes the periphery in reaction to translational and/or angular velocity, but it can affect presence.

An asymmetric mask is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that is considered an adaptive restrictor because it obscures peripheral regions with higher optical flow during virtual locomotion while leaving regions with lower optical flow visible, so it adapts based on optical flow.

A side restrictor, described as an asymmetric mask, is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy that obscures only one side of the periphery during virtual rotation and laterally shifts the center of restriction in the direction of the turn, providing a controlled way of restriction.
A ground visible restrictor is a field of view (FOV) adjustment strategy in which the ground plane remains visible during movement.

Optical-flow manipulation is a cybersickness (CS) reduction technique that can involve visually mixing optical-flow patterns in the reverse direction of virtual visual motion, using a restricted field of view (FOV) aligned with optical flow, or reducing perceived optical flow by geometrical simplification of the virtual environment.
Field of view (FOV) is the view frustum, that is, the region visible to the human eye, and it is an angular measure of what can be seen at a single point in time.

The human eye has an approximately 180-degree horizontal field of view (FOV) and a 150-degree vertical field of view, and within the 180-degree horizontal range a person sees things using both central and peripheral vision.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

concepts.name: cybersickness
concepts.definition: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

defining_facts.text: Cybersickness (CS), also known in the literature as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR) technology and is primarily relevant to virtual reality.

A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.
Cybersickness (CS) can be caused by many factors, not by a single factor.

Reducing the impact of cybersickness (CS) is very important for usability and acceptability of virtual reality (VR) systems because it greatly enhances overall user experience and makes virtual reality applications more appealing to a wider range of people.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.

A sensory mismatch in a virtual reality (VR) system may be insignificant if the user's brain can adapt, but for other users it can cause cybersickness, with symptoms such as fatigue, headache, dizziness, and nausea.

Cybersickness, also known as visually induced motion sickness (VIMS), is a condition that can affect individuals when they interact with virtual reality (VR), and it is not a single-factor effect because a variety of factors can affect it.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Finding feasible solutions to reduce the impact of cybersickness while a user is experiencing virtual reality (VR) is important because it is supposed to greatly enhance overall user experience and make VR more appealing to a wider range of people.

Cybersickness mitigation strategies often come at the cost of presence because reducing cybersickness may make the user feel more in an artificial environment than in a real environment and less likely to obtain a proper immersive experience.

concepts.name: internal factors
concepts.definition: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

defining_facts.text: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Internal factors for cyber sickness are individual characteristics and conditions inherent to users that can increase the likelihood of experiencing cyber sickness, including age, gender, motion sickness (MS) susceptibility, physical condition, and emotional condition.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

concepts.name: external factors
concepts.definition: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

defining_facts.text: The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

The causes of cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, such as age and gender, and external factors, which are divided into hardware factors, such as display type, latency, latency jitter, resolution, and input technology, and content factors.
Virtual reality (VR) content is an external factor among the causes of cybersickness.

The factors that can induce cybersickness are broadly divided into internal factors, which include the age of the user, the gender of the user, the user's susceptibility to motion sickness, the physical condition of the user, and the emotional condition of the user, and external factors, which include hardware factors such as display resolution, latency, latency jitter, type of display, and type of input, and virtual reality (VR) content factors such as visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

concepts.name: latency
concepts.definition: Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.

defining_facts.text: Latency in virtual reality (VR) is the time delay, or time gap, between a user's movement in the physical world and the corresponding change in the virtual world.
In head-mounted display (HMD)-based virtual reality (VR), cybersickness (CS) increases with latency; the more latency there is, the more likely it is to induce cybersickness.
Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

concepts.name: latency jitter
concepts.definition: Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.

defining_facts.text: Latency jitter is variability in latency, meaning that the time gap between a physical-world action and its virtual-world reflection changes from time to time.
Latency jitter causes irregularities in the timing of data delivery and can lead to inconsistencies, discomfort, disorientation, and cybersickness (CS).

concepts.name: visual motion
concepts.definition: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

defining_facts.text: The six virtual reality (VR) content factors that affect cyber sickness (CS) are visual motion, means of locomotion, field of view, type of content, duration, and visual complexity.

Visual motion, the movement experienced by a user in a virtual reality (VR) environment, is considered one of the primary causes of cyber sickness (CS), and higher visual motion can increase the risk of cyber sickness while the way the content moves also affects cyber sickness and its severity.

Vection is the sensation of self-motion, is highest when motion is sensed in peripheral stimuli, and is positively correlated with visual motion stimulus, indicating that visual motion plays a crucial role in the onset and severity of cyber sickness (CS).
Brief exposure to turbulent visual motion alone is not enough to induce cyber sickness (CS), but longer exposure to turbulent visual motion can induce cyber sickness.

concepts.name: means of locomotion
concepts.definition: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

defining_facts.text: Means of locomotion, meaning how a user moves in a virtual world, is a content-related factor in cybersickness (CS), because a sensory mismatch between virtual and physical movements can cause discomfort and disorientation that lead to cybersickness.

Control over motion in a virtual world, meaning whether and how a user controls movement, is an aspect of locomotion that directly affects presence and indirectly affects cybersickness (CS) through presence; greater presence in virtual reality (VR) generally reduces cybersickness, and more control means greater presence and less control means lower presence.

The type of transition, meaning how the scene changes from one field of view to another, is another aspect of locomotion that affects cybersickness (CS); teleportation, an instantaneous transition, is found to reduce cybersickness compared with naturalistic free movement such as walking, running, and jumping.

concepts.name: visual complexity
concepts.definition: Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

defining_facts.text: Visual complexity is an external factor that is positively correlated with cybersickness (CS) symptoms, so scenes with more objects of different shapes, sizes, and movements are more likely to induce cybersickness.

concepts.name: gait negation technique
concepts.definition: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

defining_facts.text: Walking-based locomotion is broadly divided into three categories: full gait techniques, partial gait techniques, and gait negation techniques.

Gait negation techniques require a specialized setup that cancels the user's lateral movements and keeps the user's physical position fixed, because natural walking involves lateral movement that may be difficult to map to a focused virtual movement, and the setup detects and eliminates the lateral movement before the movement is mapped to virtual navigation, making it easier for the system to understand the user's intention.
Some examples of specialized setups used in gait negation techniques are a linear treadmill, motorized floor tiles, a human-sized hamster ball, and a friction-free platform.
